title: Yashoda looks into Krishna's mouth
hookLine: a mother looks into her toddler's mouth and sees the whole universe

cards: In the village of Vraja, the little boys come running to Yashoda: Krishna ate dirt! She takes her son by the hand. Did you?
No, Mother, they're making it up. Then open your mouth. He does.

And Yashoda looks in and sees everything: the sky, the stars, mountains and oceans, fire and wind, the moon, the whole earth, and on it the village of Vraja, and in the village, herself, looking into a mouth.
The Bhagavata says she was shaken to the core. Then the vision closed, and she pulled her boy into her lap, just her son again.

teach.h: NOTHING ADDED. A COVERING CAME OFF.
teach.b: Nothing was added to Yashoda in that moment. The universe had been there all along. A covering came off.
Patanjali's last chapter makes that the fruit of the whole path. Sutra 4.30: tatah klesha-karma-nivrittih. From the cloud of dharma, the afflictions and karma cease.
The kleshas are the five from the second chapter: not-seeing, the I-am feeling, clinging to pleasure, pushing away pain, and clinging to life.
And Patanjali names the root of them all: avidya, not-seeing. That's a big Hindu idea. The deepest problem isn't that you're bad.
It's that you can't see what's really there. Then 4.31: tada sarva-avarana-mala-apetasya jnanasya anantyaj jneyam alpam.
Then, because knowledge, free of every covering and impurity, is without limit, what remains to be known is little. Avarana is a covering, like a lid. Mala is grime, the dust on a lamp's glass.
Knowledge was never small; it was covered. For Yashoda the lid came back down: the Bhagavata says Krishna veiled it again in a mother's love, so she could go on being his mother.

teach.h: FOR THE YOGI, THE LID STAYS OFF.
teach.b: For the yogi of 4.30, it stays off. And jneyam alpam, the knowable is little, isn't a claim to know every fact in the world. It's proportion.
Next to a light without limits, everything else looks small. You know the small version: a test, a fight, a fear that filled the whole room, until the room opened onto a bigger sky.

how: Commentators on the Yoga Sutras read 4.30–4.31 as the fruit of the whole path: the five kleshas of the second chapter, and the karma they drive, come to an end, and knowledge is uncovered.

o: affliction, like not-seeing or clinging to life
a stain on the soul from breaking a vow
a bad deed that must be paid back later

games.q: the mouth and the sutra — tap the pairs.
p: sees the universe in a mouth
what's left to know is little

s: 4.31 means the yogi knows every fact in the world
it's proportion: next to knowledge without limits, the knowable looks small.
for Patanjali, the root of the afflictions is not-seeing
avidya is the field the other kleshas grow in (2.4).
in the Bhagavata, Krishna's mouth held only a little dirt
Yashoda saw the whole universe in it, Vraja and herself included.

games.q: every covering and impurity is gone from knowledge. what does 4.31 say about what is left to know?
games.why: jneyam alpam: because knowledge is now without limit, what remains to be known is little.

practice: Hold lightly one thing you've been trying hard to figure out, a decision, a person, a worry. Then let your attention widen: the room, the building, the sky over it, the whole spread of the day.
Let the question sit inside all that space, smaller than it was, with nothing to solve right now.

wordCard.voice: Klesha, affliction, rooted in avidya, not-seeing. From the cloud of dharma, the kleshas and karma cease, knowledge is uncovered and without limit, and little remains to be known.

orig.note: Sanskrit alpa: little, small. jñeyam alpam, the knowable is little.

carryVoice: Your line: knowledge was covered, never small. Yashoda saw it all in a little boy's mouth. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.8.32–10.8.45 (the boys say Krishna ate dirt; Yashoda sees the universe in his mouth; he veils it in a mother's love)
Yoga Sutras 2.4–2.5 (avidya as the field of the other kleshas; what avidya is)
